problem: Robot navigation depends on prior preparation (satellite base stations and recorded routes in crop rows; surveyed maps and fixed object categories indoors), and crop-row detectors are fitted to one crop and give steering commands rather than positions.
motivation: Humans navigate with only the scene in view plus prior knowledge of spatial structure and object semantics. The dissertation builds navigation systems on the same basis, each modeling its site while working in it, within onboard compute limits. Agriculture exploits known planting geometry; indoor navigation exploits VLM semantic knowledge grounded in a self-built map.
key_idea: Use structural priors (row-planting geometry outdoors, VLM semantic knowledge grounded in an onboard-built map indoors) and arbitrate among several competent navigation experts (contextual bandit or LLM agent) instead of relying on preparation or a single strategy.
insight: Per the abstract, planting geometry (a pencil of rows converging to a vanishing point) is crop-independent, so one weight set covers nine crop domains and matches or edges nine per-domain specialists. Indoors, no single expert is best at every step, so arbitrating among experts (bandit or tool-calling LLM agent) yields high success, and the LLM agent gets the best path efficiency without navigation training. Only the abstract was available, so ablations are not visible.
method: AgroNav: composes semantic segmentation with semantic line detection to recover the two aisle-bounding lines and the centerline from one RGB frame; trained on a few hundred images, released with the AgroScapes dataset
Vanishing-point row pencil: replaces the two lines with the full set of rows converging to a shared vanishing point, so one weight set covers nine crop domains
Row-Alignment-based Bundle Adjustment (RA-BA): reads heading from the row pencil and recovers a headland turn's net rotation from the boustrophedon field topology, giving monocular visual odometry
RoboAtlas: builds an instance-level semantic map onboard and arbitrates frontier, semantic-map, and egocentric VLM experts with a contextual bandit
Argonaut: an LLM agent calls each expert as a tool and states its reason; needs no navigation training and accepts new experts without retraining

setting.backbone: Segmentation and line-detection networks (AgroNav, row-pencil detector); VLMs and a contextual bandit (RoboAtlas); an LLM agent (Argonaut, no navigation training)
setting.training_data: AgroNav: a few hundred annotated orchard images (AgroScapes); row-pencil model: multi-crop data across nine domains; Argonaut: none (no navigation training)
setting.observation: Monocular RGB for agriculture; onboard RGB(-D) with an instance-level semantic map indoors
setting.action_space: Steering commands along the row centerline (agriculture); frontier/semantic-map/egocentric-VLM expert-selected navigation goals (indoor)

numbers.extra: Split is not stated in the abstract; val-unseen is assumed

numbers_note: Abstract only; the GOAT-Bench split is not stated and the zero-shot flag is uncertain. The other results are agriculture metrics: 93.3% mean per-row autonomy over 1398 m, and 1.0 m visual odometry accuracy over seven crops.
results: RoboAtlas reaches 90.6% success on GOAT-Bench and maps two office floors on a legged robot. Argonaut reaches the best path efficiency of any evaluated system. AgroNav drives 25 orchard rows (1398 m) at 93.3% mean per-row autonomy, and the row-pencil model matches or edges nine per-domain specialists.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so baselines and ablations are not visible
The agricultural methods rely on regular planting geometry and do not transfer to unstructured settings
The indoor systems rely on VLM quality and on the set of available experts
